prize_parts.citation: for empirical analysis of how exposure to trade and technological change reshapes local labour markets, employment and wage inequality

statement.case_for: I keep B038 first, with the same three names, but I narrow the citation. My round 1 wording added a conceptual task-and-labour-demand element. The exchange showed that this is the part of the entry that is hardest to attribute to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The contribution I would credit is the measurement and causal analysis of how import and technology exposure change employment, wages and adjustment across local labour markets. It combined newly assembled data with a research design that the field now treats as standard. It also showed that adjustment costs are concentrated and persistent, which changed both research and the policy debate on globalisation and automation. Autor links this evidence to the task view of labour demand. The citation can acknowledge that link without claiming the task framework for the trio. More than a decade of replication, critique and extension means durability can be judged, which is not yet possible for the youngest candidates. The narrowed citation also answers the chair's first question. The empirical core belongs to Autor, Dorn and Hanson, and Dorn is a full co-author of the central papers. Katz's wage-structure and education-technology work is a different strand, and it would be credited properly in a differently framed prize. I did not change my ranking because of support counts. The chair's summary shows dispersed first choices and no configuration near six votes. I read that as a reason to state the case plainly, not to look for consensus.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that B038 still bundles two programmes. Even with a narrow citation, a reader may expect the task framework to be credited, and its lineage includes Levy, Murnane and Acemoglu. The persistence and magnitude of the China-shock effects remain debated, and the shift-share identification strategy has been criticised. I read that debate as refinement and not refutation, but Friberg, Krusell and Strömberg treat it as a real discount, and I cannot show they are wrong. The topic also sits near recent prizes: Goldin's 2023 prize on labour markets, which I presented, and the 2024 and 2025 prizes that colleagues cite on institutions and technology. I think the object and design differ, but a reasonable member could weigh the proximity more heavily. The three-name cap leaves out Katz, who made major contributions to the wage-structure literature. Finally, my own field is quasi-experimental labour economics, which makes B038 and B002 familiar to me. I discount my confidence for that.

responses.point: Fredriksson moved from Autor, Hanson and Katz to Autor, Hanson and Dorn. He anchors the citation in the trade-exposure and local-labour-market evidence, and he declines to claim the whole task framework for the trio.
responses.response: This is the convergence I find useful, because it rests on attribution and not on counting. We now agree on the three names and on the principle that the citation should not over-claim the task literature. I have revised my own wording to match, dropping the conceptual element. We still weigh two things differently. I read the shift-share debate as having improved practice without overturning the main finding, and he appears to treat the magnitudes as somewhat more open. The gap between us is small. I also note that he ranks B013 as a close alternative, and I do not think B038 and B013 compete on a common footing: one rests on measurement and design, the other on theory with mixed empirical tests.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B030 first and B038 seventh. He doubts that shift-share identification withstands scrutiny, says the task framework owes much to unlisted scholars, and prefers a citation limited to the China-shock evidence.
responses.response: His last point is now built into my citation, so part of our disagreement is resolved. We still differ on identification. The critique concerns how exposure designs should be built and how inference should be done. The finding of large, concentrated and persistent local adjustment costs has held up across outcomes, pre-trend checks and later designs. I accept that Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes have a very clean attribution and decades of use, and I would not call B030 weak. Where I part from him is that a methods contribution, however widely used, tells us less about how the economy works than a measured discovery with its own policy consequences. I accept his point that this is a judgement about criteria and not an objective ranking.

responses.point: Dreber added Friedman to Chetty and Hendren on B002. She says restricted data access should be a real discount on maturity, and she accepts that the Committee could rank B001 or B038 higher on durability.
responses.response: Her treatment of the access constraint is the most honest on the table, and it is the main reason I keep B002 as my first alternative and not my first choice. She says replication has to come from other designs and data environments, and I agree that this is weaker than open-data replication. Her move to Friedman also changes my view. A Chetty, Hendren and Friedman version is more coherent than a two-name list for a prize on population-data measurement. If B038 does not advance, I would support that version. I would not do so at the expense of a mature candidate, because the long-run causal reading of place effects is still being tested.

responses.point: Teorell, who ranks B002 first, argues that the causal claims rest on movers designs and the re-analysis of an experiment, which can be assessed on their logic even when the data are restricted. He also now limits a B038 prize to the trade-shock core.
responses.response: That is a fair answer to part of my data-access concern, and I have softened it. A movers design can be judged on its identifying assumptions without access to the files, so the restriction matters most for the descriptive atlas and for checks on stability. It does not matter equally for every claim. The remaining difference is timing. The causal place-effect estimates are about a decade old and still being tested for long-run robustness, while the China-shock design has been through a longer cycle of independent critique. I am glad that his B038 trio matches mine and that he wants the citation limited. The difference between us is mainly maturity, not quality.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B013 first and now says Autor, Hanson and Dorn is the more defensible grouping if B038 advances. He still worries about overlap with the 2024 prize and about China-shock magnitudes.
responses.response: I appreciate his moving to Dorn, and I think his two remaining concerns are fair. On the 2024 prize, the narrow citation should help. It describes an empirical analysis of exposure and adjustment, while the recognised institutions work concerns long-run determinants of prosperity. On magnitudes, I would distinguish them from the discovery itself. I also take his defence of B013 seriously. A prize rewards the idea and its consequences, not the survival of every prediction. My reservation is that the Protection for Sale tests are mixed, and Helpman's presence on B041 makes the B013 citation harder to frame. I rank B013 behind B038 on those grounds, not because I think it is weak.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee will accept a citation confined to the empirical analysis of trade and technology exposure, and whether that is enough to settle Dorn over Katz for members who still want a wage-structure prize.
How persistent and how externally valid the China-shock effects are, and whether continuing refinement of shift-share designs will change how the core results are read.
Whether proximity to the 2023 prize, which I presented, and to the 2024 and 2025 prizes colleagues cite reduces the room for B038 in a way I am discounting too heavily.

Whether the long-run causal neighbourhood-effect estimates in B002 will hold up, and how much restricted data access should discount them. I would support Chetty, Hendren and Friedman if B002 advances.

How to compare conceptual mechanisms with mixed direct empirical tests (B001, B012, B013) against empirical programmes with debated magnitudes (B038, B002) without field familiarity deciding the comparison.
My assessments rely on the supplied evidence and general knowledge, without independent source verification.
statement.conflict_note: No candidate-specific connection is apparent from the supplied profile. None of my listed frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) is credited on any shortlisted entry. I work in labour economics with quasi-experimental methods, which is close to B038 and B002, and I treat that as field familiarity, not as evidence of merit. I presented the 2023 prize (Goldin) at the announcement. That speech reflects Academy drafting and does not show a preference for any 2026 candidate, though it is relevant to the prior-prize overlap I discuss. I sit on the Board of Editors of the American Economic Review, and shortlisted candidates may publish in it. I have no personal tie to any of them. These ties are disclosed and not adjudicated.
